strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper correctly distinguishes storage compression from rendering-memory compression, a genuinely under-explored angle in 3DGS compression, and analyzes the static vs. dynamic VRAM components sensibly.

Solid technical approach: replacing SH with arbitrarily-oriented Spherical Gaussians plus a unified ADMM-based soft pruning of both primitives and lobes is a coherent design, and the color compensation term (Eq. 15) is derived cleanly.

Comprehensive evaluation: comparisons across Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, and Deep Blending against a broad set of baselines (3DGS, SG-Splatting, GaussianSpa, Mini-Splatting, Reduced3DGS, VQ/neural-compression methods, HAC++/Scaffold-GS), with static and rendering VRAM both reported.

Thorough ablations that directly test each design choice (SG vs. SH vs. ortho-axis SG, soft vs. hard, unified vs. sequential pruning, color compensation, and naive combinations of existing methods), plus convincing real-device demos (WebGL on mobile SoCs) that substantiate the practical motivation.
Results are strong: ~2x further VRAM reduction over GaussianSpa at comparable or better quality, and clearly better quality-memory trade-off than VQ/entropy methods that must decode before rendering.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: both core ingredients are extensions of prior work — the SG color model builds on SG-Splatting (Wang et al., 2024b), and the unified soft pruning is a direct extension of GaussianSpa's ADMM formulation from primitive-count pruning to a joint primitive+lobe budget. The contribution is more integration/engineering than a fundamentally new method.
Some baseline VRAM numbers are estimated rather than measured (LP-3DGS, Mini-Splatting values extrapolated from 3DGS/GaussianSpa measurements), which weakens the VRAM comparisons in Table 1.
Table 1 contains an unexplained second 'Ours' row (e.g., 27.21/40MB on Mip-NeRF360) whose configuration, quality-memory trade-off, and purpose are never described in the text.

Rendering quality on Mip-NeRF360 PSNR is slightly below GaussianSpa (27.54 vs 27.56) and on Tanks&Temples below both 3DGS and GaussianSpa (23.57 vs 23.73), so the 'comparable or even improving quality' claim should be stated more carefully; per-scene breakdowns are not provided.

Missing details affect reproducibility and assessment: training time/compute cost of the ADMM optimization is not reported, sensitivity to the budget κ and penalty δ is not analyzed, and dynamic VRAM is admittedly not optimized (Limitation), which somewhat weakens the 'solves the memory bottleneck' claim given dynamic VRAM still scales with primitive count.
The memory analysis (Section 2.2, Sec. 1) is qualitative and heuristic; no formal model or measurement study of static/dynamic VRAM composition is provided to support the two-factor decomposition.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: rendering-time VRAM (not just storage) of 3DGS, and provides a reasonable decomposition of memory into static and dynamic components, which is a useful framing.

The empirical results are solid: consistent VRAM reductions over a broad set of baselines (pruning, quantization, and anchor-based methods) across standard benchmarks, with comparable or slightly better rendering quality.

Ablations are relatively thorough, covering the color representation (SH vs. orthogonal vs. arbitrary SG), soft vs. hard lobe pruning, unified vs. sequential pruning, and the color compensation term, plus a comparison against naive combinations of existing techniques.
The demonstration on mobile platforms (Figure 1) supports the practical motivation of edge-device rendering.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. Both core ingredients are adaptations of existing work: spherical Gaussians as a color representation largely follow SG-Splatting (Wang et al., 2024b), and the unified pruning is a direct extension of GaussianSpa's ADMM sparsification framework from opacity to opacity+sharpness. The proximal operators for opacity are explicitly reused from GaussianSpa. The contribution is closer to a careful combination than a new technique.

The claimed contrast between this work and prior 'storage-only' compression is somewhat overstated. Several prior works (e.g., reduced-attribute and pruning-based methods) also reduce rendering memory; the paper's positioning could be more measured.

Some headline claims are not consistently supported: on Tanks & Temples the method's PSNR (23.57) is clearly below GaussianSpa (23.73), and Table 1 contains two unlabeled rows for 'Ours' whose distinction and configurations are never explained in the text.

Measurement methodology is inconsistent across baselines: VRAM for several pruning baselines is *estimated* from primitive counts and the authors' own measurements for other methods, rather than directly measured, which weakens the precision of the core memory comparisons.

No quantitative quality evaluation is provided on the mobile/edge devices used for the motivating FPS demo; the edge claim rests only on frame rates in Figure 1 without fidelity metrics, so the quality-vs-memory trade-off on target platforms is unverified.
No statement about code release or reproducibility; given the reliance on reproduced baselines and estimated VRAM numbers, reproducibility is a concern.

Writing quality issues reduce clarity: 'Memory-contrained' in Figure 2, 'Gausian' in the method overview, the unexplained dual rows in Table 1, and hyperbolic language ('unprecedented', 'fundamentally solves') that is stronger than the evidence.

The framework does not address the dynamic VRAM component despite the introduction's claim that both matter; this admitted limitation weakens the central 'rendering memory bottleneck' narrative for memory-constrained renderers where dynamic overhead dominates.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and relatively under-explored problem: rendering VRAM (as opposed to storage) compression for 3DGS, with a clear analysis decomposing memory into static and dynamic components.

The core idea of jointly optimizing primitive count and per-primitive parameters via a single memory-constrained optimization problem (unified soft pruning of opacity and SG lobe sharpness with an ADMM-inspired solver) is technically sound and cleanly formulated (Eq. 6-13).

The replacement of spherical harmonics with arbitrarily-oriented spherical Gaussians, plus an exact closed-form color compensation term (Eq. 15) for removed lobes, is elegant and empirically validated.

Comprehensive evaluation across Mip-NeRF360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending with a broad set of baselines spanning pruning, VQ/neural compression, and anchor-based methods, including a direct VRAM comparison against HAC++/Scaffold-GS.

Thorough ablations (Table 4, Figure 3) that isolate the contribution of SG color representation, unified vs. sequential pruning, soft vs. hard pruning, and color compensation, including comparisons against naive combinations of existing methods.

Practical relevance is demonstrated with a WebGL viewer showing real-time rendering on mobile SoCs (Figure 1), and VRAM measurement methodology is carefully described (static vs. rendering, PyTorch-based accounting).
weaknesses: The core machinery is heavily built on GaussianSpa (Zhang et al., 2025b): the ADMM sparsification framework, opacity proximal operators, and training schedule are reused, so the novelty is largely in extending the constraint from primitive count to a weighted memory budget and applying it to SG sharpness. This incremental relationship could be more explicitly and honestly positioned.

Two unlabeled rows for 'Ours' in Table 1 (and multiple points in Figure 3) without clear explanation of what they represent (presumably different memory budgets) make the main results harder to interpret; the quality-vs-budget trade-off curve should be explicitly presented.

VRAM figures for some baselines (LP-3DGS, Mini-Splatting) are estimated from reported primitive counts rather than directly measured, which introduces potential unfairness in the headline claims; the authors should report measured values or clearly flag estimates.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: 'unprecedented memory compression' and the framing as 'fundamentally solving the memory bottleneck' (conclusion) overstate the contribution; rendering VRAM reduction over GaussianSpa (~40%) is solid but not transformative.

Edge-device claims rest on Figure 1 alone; no systematic mobile evaluation (latency distributions, memory ceilings, diverse scenes) or comparison with mobile-optimized renderers is provided, and the limitation section concedes dynamic VRAM is not modeled in the optimization.

No mention of code release, and several reproduction details are unclear (how the budget κ is chosen per dataset, sensitivity to hyperparameters δ, η, thresholds for post-processing), which limits reproducibility.
The abstract's '50% static VRAM reduction' vs. the introduction's '8x' compression are different baselines and could confuse readers; consistency in reporting is needed.
